items.question: What does the word "prehistory" mean to historians?
items.answer: The long time in the past before people invented writing or kept written records
items.explanation: Because prehistoric people left no letters or books, we learn about them from buried objects, bones, and footprints.

items.question: How do archaeologists find out how prehistoric families lived without any written books?
items.answer: By carefully digging up surviving clues like stone tools, animal bones, and ancient camps
items.explanation: Archaeologists act like detectives, piecing together everyday life from clues preserved underground.

items.question: On a history timeline, which date happened earlier (longer ago): 8000 BC or 2000 BC?
items.explanation: BC dates count backwards towards 1 BC, so bigger BC numbers happened much earlier in time!

items.question: Why do archaeologists find millions of prehistoric stone tools underground, but no plastic or iron ones from the Stone Age?
items.answer: Stone Age people had not discovered metal or plastic yet, and hard stone does not rot away
items.explanation: Wooden handles and animal skins usually rot in soil, while chipped flint stays sharp for hundreds of thousands of years.

items.question: Look at a map of Britain today: is modern Britain joined to mainland Europe by dry land, or surrounded by sea as an island?
items.answer: Surrounded by sea as an island
items.explanation: Today the English Channel and North Sea separate Britain from mainland Europe — though in the Ice Age you could walk across!

narrative_blocks.title: c. 850,000–10,000 BC: Ice Age Caves, Flint Handaxes & Mammoth Hunters
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.1] Long before written books, early humans lived through a huge age called **prehistory**. Around **850,000 BC**, barefoot families left footprints in wet mud at **Happisburgh** in Norfolk. During the **Palaeolithic**, or **Old Stone Age**, thick ice sheets covered northern Britain. Hunters sheltered from freezing winds inside deep limestone caves like **Creswell Crags**.

[1.2] Nobody had metal tools yet, so makers struck flint rocks to chip sharp flakes. Craftworkers called this clever stone-shaping skill **knapping**, making tear-drop **handaxes** to chop meat and wood. Brave teams worked together to track giant **woolly mammoths** and wild horses. One mammoth gave warm furry hides for clothes, lamp fat, and strong bones.

narrative_blocks.title: c. 10,000–7000 BC: Warming Forests, Cheddar Man & Star Carr
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.3] Around **10,000 BC**, the bitter Ice Age ended and the **Mesolithic**, or **Middle Stone Age**, began. Melting ice left green forests filled with red deer, wild boar, and hazelnuts. Small **hunter-gatherer** groups moved camp each season to fish clear rivers and pick berries. Inside **Gough's Cave** in Somerset, archaeologists found the skeleton of **Cheddar Man**.

[1.4] Scientists tested his ancient skull and learned he had dark skin, dark curls, and blue eyes. Farther north at **Star Carr** in Yorkshire, families built wooden lakeside platforms. Makers there carved **red-deer antler headdresses** with strap holes for hunting disguises or special dances.

narrative_blocks.title: c. 6500–4000 BC: Rising Seas & the Sinking of Doggerland
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.5] For thousands of years, hunters walked straight from Europe to Britain across dry land. Historians call this lost green land bridge **Doggerland**, where rivers wound through marshes and woods. Families camped beside Doggerland's pools to spear eels, net ducks, and trap beavers.

[1.6] Yet melting northern ice sheets kept pouring huge amounts of water into the sea. Around **6500 BC**, rising waves and storms flooded the low valleys of Doggerland forever. Today, fishing boats drag mammoth teeth and flint spear tips from the **North Sea** seabed. Sinking Doggerland cut Britain off from mainland Europe and made our home an island!

tasks.model_answer: During the Ice Age and early Mesolithic, Britain was not an island yet because a wide green land bridge called Doggerland joined Britain straight to mainland Europe. Hunter-gatherer families walked across Doggerland’s marshes and woods to spear eels, net ducks, and track deer. However, as giant northern ice sheets melted, rising waters and storms flooded Doggerland around 6500 BC, cutting Britain off as an island. Even today, fishing boats in the North Sea drag up mammoth teeth and flint spear tips from that sunken landscape!

tasks.question: Big Question: How did Old and Middle Stone Age hunter-gatherers survive in Britain, and how did Britain become an island?
tasks.starter: Between the icy Palaeolithic and the warmer Mesolithic, Stone Age life in Britain changed hugely...
hints: Describe Palaeolithic survival first (Happisburgh footprints, Creswell Crags caves, tear-drop handaxes, and woolly mammoths).

tasks.model_answer: Between the icy Palaeolithic and the warmer Mesolithic, Stone Age life in Britain changed hugely. In the freezing Old Stone Age, early humans left footprints at Happisburgh, sheltered inside caves like Creswell Crags, chipped flint handaxes, and hunted giant woolly mammoths. Once the ice melted around 10,000 BC, green Mesolithic forests spread across Britain, where seasonal hunter-gatherers like Cheddar Man and Star Carr families hunted red deer, gathered hazelnuts, and fished lakes. Finally, rising seas drowned Doggerland around 6500 BC, turning Britain into an island!

narrative_blocks.title: c. 4000–3500 BC: Boats Across the Sea & the First British Farms
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.1] Around **4000 BC**, families paddling boats across the sea brought big new ideas to island Britain. Historians call this age the **Neolithic**, or **New Stone Age**, when people began **farming**. Settlers brought tame **sheep**, **pigs**, and **cattle**, plus bags of **wheat** and **barley** seeds. None of those farm animals or grain crops grew wild in Britain before!

[2.2] First, villagers chopped down thick forests using smooth **polished stone axes** in wooden handles. Next, farmers planted seeds and sliced ripe crops with curved flint **sickles**. Potters also coiled wet clay into round **pottery** bowls for boiling hot stews. Because farms grew steady food, families stayed in permanent **thatched villages** all year.

narrative_blocks.title: c. 3100 BC & 1850: The Storm That Uncovered Skara Brae in Orkney
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.3] In winter **1850**, a fierce storm whipped away sand dunes on **Orkney**, off northern Scotland. Beneath the grass lay **Skara Brae**, a hidden Neolithic village built around **3100 BC**! Few trees grew on windy Orkney, so villagers stacked flat stones to build eight houses. Covered passages linked the homes together so neighbours stayed dry during winter gales.

[2.4] Stepping inside Skara Brae feels like visiting a Stone Age home frozen in time. Each room still has **stone box beds** once stuffed with soft heather and sheepskins. Families cooked over a central **hearth**, placed treasures on a **stone dresser**, and used indoor **drains**!

narrative_blocks.title: c. 3650–2500 BC: Ancestor Tombs at West Kennet Long Barrow
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.5] Settled farming families also worked together to honour dead ancestors on high hills. Around **3650 BC**, villagers in Wiltshire built **West Kennet Long Barrow**, a long chalk mound. Heavy standing boulders guarded five dark stone chambers tucked inside its eastern entrance.

[2.6] Over many lifetimes, families carried the bones of nearly fifty people inside. Mourners left hand-coiled clay bowls, bone pins, and beads beside their loved ones. Neighbours also gathered outside the stone entrance for seasonal ceremonies and shared feasts. Giant **long barrows** showed travellers that farming communities belonged to that land forever.

tasks.model_answer: When Neolithic farming arrived across the sea around 4000 BC, everyday life changed completely because families no longer relied only on chasing wild deer or picking berries. Because Britain was now an island, pioneer farmers paddled boats carrying sheep, pigs, cattle, and wheat and barley seeds. After chopping down trees with polished stone axes, families grew steady harvests and stored grain for winter, allowing them to live year-round in thatched or stone villages and honour ancestors in long barrows.

tasks.question: Big Question: How did farming transform everyday Stone Age life, and what does Skara Brae reveal about Neolithic homes?
tasks.starter: Historians view the switch to Neolithic farming around 4000 BC as a giant turning point because...
hints: Explain how polished stone axes reshaped Britain’s thick wild forests into sunny fields and pastures.
Use Skara Brae to prove that settled farming led to permanent homes, furniture, and pottery.

tasks.model_answer: Historians view the switch to Neolithic farming around 4000 BC as a giant turning point because people began reshaping Britain’s landscape instead of just following wild herds. Using polished stone axes and flint sickles, farmers cleared forests to raise sheep and cattle and harvest wheat. Permanent food supplies let communities build snug stone homes with beds and dressers like Skara Brae, craft clay pots, and unite to raise monumental ancestor tombs like West Kennet Long Barrow!

narrative_blocks.title: c. 3000–2500 BC: Antler Picks, Chalk Henges & Welsh Bluestones
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.1] Nobody built **Stonehenge** in one summer, as families worked on Salisbury Plain for centuries! Around **3000 BC**, workers dug a round chalk ditch and bank called a **henge**. Teams had no metal spades, so they chipped white chalk with **red-deer antler picks**. Workers scooped loose rubble into baskets using flat cattle shoulder bones as shovels. Villagers buried the cremated ashes of respected ancestors inside holes around the chalk ring.

[3.2] Later, around **2500 BC**, builders hauled eighty spotted **bluestones** from the **Preseli Hills** in Wales. Dragging those heavy rocks **140 miles** over hills and rivers took amazing teamwork and plant ropes!

narrative_blocks.title: c. 2500 BC: 25-Tonne Sarsen Trilithons & Durrington Walls Village
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.3] Next came giant grey **sarsen** boulders, each weighing **twenty-five tonnes** like four elephants! Workers had no wheels or cranes, so teams pulled stones twenty miles on **wooden sledges** and **rollers**. Craftworkers pounded every hard sarsen block smooth using heavy round stone hammer-balls. Builders tipped tall uprights into deep pits and levered heavy capstones across the top.

[3.4] Each three-stone arch, called a **trilithon**, locked tight with stone peg-and-hole **mortise-and-tenon** joints! Two miles away at **Durrington Walls**, hundreds of builders slept inside warm chalk-walled houses. Huge heaps of pig and cattle bones prove families gathered there for winter feasts. Roasted meat fed hungry workers after frosty days hauling massive stones across Wiltshire.

narrative_blocks.title: c. 2500–2200 BC: The Heel Stone & Solstice Sun Alignments
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.5] Why did Neolithic communities work without metal tools to raise Stonehenge and nearby **Avebury**? Nobody left written notes, so archaeologists study buried clues and test sky alignments. Outside the main stone circle stands a lone marker boulder called the **Heel Stone**.

[3.6] On **Midsummer** morning, the rising sun shines straight over the Heel Stone into Stonehenge! Better still, on the shortest **Midwinter** day, the setting sun glows between the tallest trilithon. Careful builders had lined the giant stones up with the sun's yearly path. Stonehenge worked as a **solar calendar**, an ancestor shrine, and a sacred healing place!

tasks.model_answer: Without wheels, horses, or metal cranes, Neolithic engineers raised Stonehenge through clever teamwork. First, teams hauled spotted bluestones 140 miles from the Preseli Hills in Wales using sledges, rafts, and twisted plant ropes. Next, hundreds of workers dragged 25-tonne grey sarsen boulders twenty miles across Wiltshire over wooden log rollers. After tipping tall uprights into deep pits, builders levered heavy capstones up timber platforms and locked each giant trilithon tight with stone peg-and-hole mortise-and-tenon joints!

tasks.question: Big Question: How did Neolithic communities build Stonehenge without wheels or metal, and why was it aligned with the sun?
tasks.starter: Because Neolithic builders left no written records, archaeologists use clues to suggest three main purposes for Stonehenge...
hints: Reason 1 — Explain the cremation burials dug into the 3000 BC chalk henge (honouring ancestors).

tasks.model_answer: Because Neolithic builders left no written records, archaeologists use clues to suggest three main purposes for Stonehenge. First, over one hundred cremation burials inside the 3000 BC chalk henge prove it began as a sacred cemetery honouring ancestors. Second, aligning the Heel Stone and tallest trilithons with Midsummer sunrise and Midwinter sunset made it a giant solar calendar marking the farming year. Third, Welsh bluestones and huge pork feasts at Durrington Walls show it united distant communities for worship and healing!

lessons.prologue: Around 2400 BC, travellers crossed the sea from Europe bringing patterned bell-shaped clay drinking pots and a dazzling secret: melting rock in roaring fires to pour liquid metal! How did mixing Welsh copper with Cornish tin create tough bronze tools, golden capes, and rich burials like the Amesbury Archer near Stonehenge?

teacher_notes.primer: This Key Stage 2 enquiry explores the technological and social shift from the New Stone Age into the Early Bronze Age (c. 2500–1200 BC). Primary pupils investigate how Beaker migrants arrived from mainland Europe around 2400 BC with bell-shaped pottery and metalworking knowledge, how miners extracted copper at Great Orme (North Wales) and tin in Cornwall, and how smiths smelted ore and alloyed nine parts copper with one part tin to cast recyclable bronze axes in two-piece moulds. Finally, pupils examine dazzling sheet-gold regalia (the Mold Gold Cape, lunulae, and Bush Barrow lozenge) alongside the Amesbury Archer — whose Alpine tooth-enamel signature proves long-distance European travel.

narrative_blocks.title: Beaker Newcomers & Mining Metal (c. 2500–2000 BC)
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] Around **2400 BC**, newcomers called the **Beaker people** sailed from Europe across the sea to Britain. Archaeologists named them after their **beakers**, which were bell-shaped clay drinking pots stamped with neat patterns. Even more excitingly, these travellers brought clever **metalworking** skills that ended the Stone Age forever!

[4.2] Early miners crawled down dark tunnels at **Great Orme** in North Wales to dig green **copper** rock. Down in **Cornwall**, workers panned cold streams and dug cliffs to gather heavy **tin** ore. Metalworkers crushed the rock and **smelted** it, melting shiny liquid metal out of stone over roaring fires.

narrative_blocks.title: Mixing Copper & Tin Into Tough Bronze (c. 2100–1500 BC)
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.3] Pure copper bent far too easily when chopping thick oak trees. Clever smiths mixed nine parts **copper** with one part **tin** to create tough golden **bronze**! They poured glowing liquid bronze into **two-piece moulds**, which were hollow stone shapes carved for axe blades. Once cooled, smiths hammered the sharp bronze edge until it gleamed.

[4.4] Unlike chipped flint that snapped forever, a broken bronze axe could be melted down and cast again. Sharp bronze axes cleared dense woodland much faster, opening wide sunny fields for barley and cattle. Communities guarding precious tin and copper routes soon grew wealthy. Bronze tools changed farming across Britain.

narrative_blocks.title: Golden Capes & The Amesbury Archer (c. 2300–1500 BC)
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.5] Master craftworkers also beat thin sheets of Welsh and Irish **gold** into dazzling treasures for chieftains. In Wales, one leader wore the **Mold Gold Cape**, hammered from a single nugget of gold! Other rulers wore crescent-moon gold neck collars called **lunulae** and diamond breastplates at **Bush Barrow**.

[4.6] Near **Stonehenge**, archaeologists found the **Amesbury Archer**, buried around **2300 BC** with over one hundred grave goods. His grave held five clay **beakers**, copper knives, flint arrowheads, stone wrist-guards, and Britain's oldest gold hair rings. Tests on his **tooth enamel** proved he grew up near the snowy **Alps**! Clearly, skilled travellers now linked Britain tightly to Europe.

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: Why did making bronze force communities in North Wales, Cornwall, and mainland Europe to trade with each other?
tasks.starter: Making bronze forced communities to trade across long distances because...
hints: Explain why pure copper bent too easily and what recipe (nine parts copper, one part tin) made hard bronze.
Name where miners dug copper (Great Orme in Wales) and where workers gathered tin (Cornwall).
Explain how controlling rare tin and copper trade routes helped create rich chieftains wearing treasures like Source C and Source D!
tasks.model_answer: Making bronze forced communities to trade across long distances because copper and tin were rarely found in the same place. Miners dug green copper rock down tunnels at Great Orme in North Wales, while workers gathered heavy tin ore far away in Cornwall. Because smiths needed nine parts copper and one part tin to cast tough bronze, boats and traders linked Wales, Cornwall, Ireland, and Europe, making leaders who guarded those trade routes wealthy enough to wear sheet-gold collars and breastplates.

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did Beaker newcomers and bronze metalworking transform life and power in Britain?
tasks.starter: Bronze metalworking transformed both everyday work and leadership in Britain because...
hints: Point 1 (Tools & Farms) — explain how sharp, recyclable bronze axes cleared dense forests for sunny fields.
Point 2 (Power & Gold) — use Source C (gold lunula), Source D (Bush Barrow gold), and the Mold Gold Cape to show rich individual chieftains.
Reach a clear judgement linking both — could chieftains have grown so rich without trade in copper, tin, and farming surpluses?
tasks.model_answer: Bronze metalworking transformed both everyday work and leadership in Britain because better tools and long-distance trade fed each other. On farms, tough bronze axes cast in two-piece moulds cleared woodland much faster than brittle flint, helping families grow more barley and raise larger herds. Even more dramatically, because tin in Cornwall and copper at Great Orme were rare, leaders who controlled metal trade and skilled guests like the Alpine-born Amesbury Archer became powerful chieftains, buried alone under round barrows near Stonehenge wearing gold lunulae and the Bush Barrow breastplate.

lessons.enquiry_question: Why do archaeologists call Must Farm "Britain's Pompeii", and what does it reveal about Bronze Age life?
lessons.prologue: Imagine stepping inside a 3,000-year-old wooden house where bowls still hold burnt porridge, wooden spoons rest inside pots, willow traps wait for eels, and Britain's oldest complete wheel lies beside the wall! Discover how a sudden fire and wet Cambridgeshire river mud froze Must Farm in time — and how sewn-plank oak boats crossed the Channel!
lessons.blurb: Imagine stepping inside a 3,000-year-old wooden house where bowls still hold burnt porridge, wooden spoons rest inside pots, willow traps wait for eels, and Britain's oldest complete wheel lies beside the wall! Discover how a sudden fire and wet Cambridgeshire river mud froze Must Farm in time — and how sewn-plank oak boats crossed the Channel!

teacher_notes.primer: This Key Stage 2 enquiry takes primary pupils inside one of Europe's most remarkable archaeological discoveries: the Late Bronze Age stilt settlement at Must Farm in Cambridgeshire (c. 900 BC), alongside nearby Flag Fen and the seagoing Dover Bronze Age Boat. Pupils learn in crystal-clear everyday language why wood, cloth, and food survived for 3,000 years (falling from a sudden fire straight into thick, airless wet river mud so nothing rotted away). Through rich domestic artefacts — porridge bowls with spoons, plant-fibre textiles, willow eel traps, hafted bronze axes, Mediterranean beads, and Britain's oldest complete 1-metre wooden wheel — pupils overturn any stereotype of prehistoric people as clumsy or isolated.

objectives.objective: Explain why Must Farm was built on wooden stilts over a river and how thick, airless wet mud preserved organic items after a fire.
objectives.primer: Contrast dry land (where wood and cloth rot away) with Must Farm's waterlogged river mud that sealed falling roundhouses around 900 BC.
objectives.question: Why do archaeologists nickname Must Farm "Britain's Pompeii" even though there was no volcano in Cambridgeshire?

objectives.objective: Use everyday finds from Must Farm — charred porridge, plant-fibre cloth, eel traps, and Britain's oldest complete wheel — to describe Bronze Age family life.
objectives.primer: Show how families combined river fishing (eel traps) with dryland farming (wheat, sheep, and wheeled carts).
objectives.question: What does finding both a willow eel trap and a 1-metre wooden cart wheel at Must Farm prove?

objectives.objective: Describe how Bronze Age shipwrights built sewn-plank oak vessels like the Dover Boat to trade across the English Channel.
objectives.primer: Examine how oak planks stitched with twisted yew withies and sealed with moss carried tin, bronze, and Mediterranean beads across the sea.
objectives.question: How did Bronze Age builders hold giant oak boat planks together without iron nails?

source_context.Source A: Normally archaeologists only ever dig up bare metal axe blades because wooden handles rot away in dry soil. At Must Farm in Cambridgeshire, thick airless river mud preserved complete ash and oak handles still slotted tightly into bronze axe sockets! **Hinge Question:** Why did wooden axe handles survive for 3,000 years at Must Farm when wood usually rots away?
source_context.Source B: When a sudden fire swept through Must Farm around 900 BC, families fled while shelves of stacked pottery crashed straight into the river below. Several bowls still held burnt wheat-and-seed porridge with a wooden stirring spoon resting inside! **Hinge Question:** Why did archaeologists nickname Must Farm "Britain's Pompeii" when they found bowls still holding food and spoons?
source_context.Source C: Living on stilts right above a slow Cambridgeshire river gave Must Farm families fresh fish on their doorstep! Villagers wove springy willow twigs into funnel baskets so eels and pike could swim easily inside but could not swim back out. **Hinge Question:** How did Must Farm families turn living above wet Fenland rivers into a clever advantage for food?
source_context.Source D: At wetlands like Rhyd-y-Gorse in Wales and Flag Fen near Must Farm, Late Bronze Age people carefully lowered gleaming bronze shields, swords, and spearheads into watery marshes and rivers, never intending to dig them back up. **Hinge Question:** Why did Bronze Age people deliberately place valuable bronze shields and swords into wet bogs and rivers?

items.question: On which two special days of the year does the sun line up directly with the Heel Stone at Stonehenge?
items.answer: Midsummer sunrise (summer solstice) and midwinter sunset (winter solstice)
items.explanation: Neolithic engineers aligned Stonehenge's Avenue and giant sarsen trilithons carefully with the solstice sun.

items.question: Which two metals did Bronze Age smiths melt together (nine parts to one part) to cast hard golden bronze?
items.answer: Copper (nine parts) and tin (one part)
items.explanation: Miners dug copper at Great Orme in North Wales and gathered tin in Cornwall to smelt and mix into tough bronze.

items.question: What bell-shaped patterned clay pots gave their name to the newcomers who arrived in Britain from Europe around 2400 BC?
items.answer: Beakers (brought by the Beaker people)
items.explanation: The Beaker people arrived from mainland Europe bringing comb-decorated clay drinking pots and early metalworking skills.

items.question: How did scientists discover that the Amesbury Archer (buried near Stonehenge around 2300 BC) grew up near the Alps?
items.answer: By testing childhood drinking-water clues locked inside his tooth enamel
items.explanation: His tooth enamel matched cold Alpine mountain water, proving long-distance travel between Europe and Bronze Age Britain.

current_items.question: Why did wood, cloth, and food survive for 3,000 years beneath the burnt roundhouses at Must Farm in Cambridgeshire?
current_items.answer: Burning houses dropped straight into thick, airless wet river mud so nothing rotted away
current_items.explanation: Without air in the deep river silt, tiny microbes could not rot wooden spoons, willow baskets, or plant-fibre cloth.

current_items.question: What wooden structure did Bronze Age builders drive across the wet marshes nearby at Flag Fen?
current_items.answer: A long timber causeway (wooden bridge road) held up by thousands of oak posts
current_items.explanation: Flag Fen's timber causeway linked dry farmland across the marshes and served as a sacred place for water offerings.

current_items.question: What record-breaking 1-metre transport object did archaeologists uncover intact in the mud at Must Farm?
current_items.answer: Britain's oldest complete wooden wheel (c. 900 BC)
current_items.explanation: Made from ash planks pinned firmly together, it proved Must Farm families used wheeled carts on nearby dry fields.

current_items.question: Which surprise mealtime clue was still sitting inside clay bowls excavated at Must Farm?
current_items.answer: Charred wheat porridge with a carved wooden spoon resting inside
current_items.explanation: Finding half-eaten meals showed how suddenly the fire forced families to evacuate their stilt homes.

current_items.question: How were the thick oak planks of the Dover Bronze Age Boat held together without any iron nails?
current_items.answer: Stitched tightly together with twisted yew branches and sealed watertight with moss
current_items.explanation: Built around 1550 BC, the sewn-plank Dover Boat carried crews and metal cargoes safely across the English Channel.

narrative_blocks.text:
[5.1] Around **900 BC**, Bronze Age families built wooden **roundhouses** at **Must Farm** in Cambridgeshire. Each home stood high on oak **stilts**, which were sturdy wooden posts driven into a slow river. Thick, airless wet mud sealed everything inside so nothing rotted away! Archaeologists soon nicknamed **Must Farm** **"Britain's Pompeii."**

narrative_blocks.title: Sacred Waters & Crossing the Channel in Oak Boats
narrative_blocks.text:
[5.5] That sturdy **wooden wheel** proved families drove carts across dry fields beside the marshes, raising sheep and harvesting wheat. Inside the burnt roundhouses, tiny **glass beads** from **Mediterranean** workshops showed how far trade reached! Meanwhile at **Flag Fen**, villagers lowered shining bronze shields and swords into sacred marsh waters.

[5.6] How did traders cross the choppy **English Channel** before iron nails existed? At **Dover** in Kent, archaeologists unearthed the **Dover Bronze Age Boat**! Shipwrights split giant **oak** planks and stitched them tightly together using twisted **yew** branches and moss. Brave crews paddled tin and bronze safely between Britain and France. Bronze Age families were skilled builders, weavers, and sea traders!

lessons.blurb: Around 800 BC, blacksmiths learned to hammer common reddish iron rock into razor-sharp ploughs and swords! Discover how booming Celtic tribes ground flour on spinning quern stones, lived in cosy thatched roundhouses, ringed hilltops with giant earth ramparts like Maiden Castle, wore twisted gold torcs, and minted gold coins right before Rome invaded in AD 43!

teacher_notes.primer: This capstone Key Stage 2 enquiry brings over 800,000 years of British prehistory to a vivid climax in the Iron Age (c. 800 BC–AD 43). Primary pupils explore why common reddish iron ore allowed every village blacksmith to forge tough ploughshares, saws, and swords without relying solely on distant tin routes. Pupils step inside smoky thatched wattle-and-daub roundhouses (rotary querns, upright looms), climb the giant chalk ramparts of Maiden Castle and the Uffington White Horse, and admire Celtic artistry (the Waterloo Horned Helmet, Snettisham Great Torc, and gold stater coins) — proving Britain on the eve of Emperor Claudius's AD 43 invasion was populous, artistic, and thriving.

objectives.objective: Explain why widespread iron ore and blacksmith forging made iron tools more common and tougher than bronze.
objectives.primer: Contrast rare Cornish tin and Welsh copper against widespread reddish iron ore hammered hot on blacksmith anvils into heavy clay ploughshares.
objectives.question: Why could far more Iron Age farmers own an iron ploughshare or sickle than earlier farmers could own bronze?

objectives.objective: Describe everyday Celtic life inside wattle-and-daub roundhouses and giant defended hillforts like Maiden Castle.
objectives.primer: Explore chimney-free thatched roundhouses, spinning rotary quern stones, upright looms, and multi-banked chalk ramparts.
objectives.question: Why didn't Iron Age roundhouses have a chimney hole at the top of the thatched roof?

objectives.objective: Synthesise changes across the Stone, Bronze, and Iron Ages using torcs, horned helmets, and gold stater coins up to AD 43.
objectives.primer: Weigh Celtic artistry (Snettisham Great Torc, Waterloo Helmet, Uffington White Horse, gold staters) and look back across the whole unit.
objectives.question: How do gold stater coins, rotary querns, and Maiden Castle prove Iron Age Britons were advanced long before AD 43?

source_context.Source A: In earlier Stone and Bronze Age homes, families knelt for hours pushing a rubbing stone back and forth on a flat saddle stone. Iron Age engineers invented the spinning rotary quern: a heavy round top stone turned with a wooden handle over a bottom stone! **Hinge Question:** How did spinning a round rotary quern stone make daily life easier for Iron Age farming families?
source_context.Source B: Dredged from the muddy bed of the River Thames in London in 1868, this unique bronze horned helmet is made from thin riveted bronze sheets decorated with swirling Celtic curves and red enamel studs. Its thin sheet metal would dent easily against an iron sword! **Hinge Question:** If the Waterloo Helmet's bronze sheet was too thin for real sword fights, why was it made and placed in the River Thames?
source_context.Source C: Ploughed up by a farmer at Snettisham in Norfolk in 1950, this heavy neck ring (torc) weighs over a kilogram! Celtic goldsmiths twisted sixty-four fine gold-and-silver threads into eight neat ropes and soldered richly patterned hollow terminals onto both ends. **Hinge Question:** What does the Snettisham Great Torc prove about the skill and wealth of Iron Age Celtic Britain BEFORE the Romans invaded?
source_context.Source D: By 100–50 BC, powerful Celtic tribes across Britain began minting their own gold, silver, and bronze coins called staters. Many stamped bold galloping horses, wheat ears, and even the names of tribal kings in Latin letters learned through cross-Channel trade! **Hinge Question:** Why does stamping gold coins and king names mark the moment British "prehistory" began turning into written history?

items.question: What stone-built New Stone Age village in Orkney was uncovered by a fierce storm in 1850 with stone beds and dressers still inside?
items.answer: Skara Brae
items.explanation: Built around 3100 BC in treeless Orkney, Skara Brae's flagstone houses and furniture survived beneath coastal sand dunes.

items.question: What do archaeologists call the giant horseshoe pairs of upright sarsen stones topped by horizontal lintels at Stonehenge?
items.answer: Trilithons (meaning "three stones")
items.explanation: Each giant sarsen trilithon locked its top lintel stone firmly onto two uprights using carved mortise-and-tenon joints.

items.question: What does "smelting" mean, and which two metals were mixed (nine parts to one part) to make bronze?
items.answer: Melting liquid metal out of rock in a hot fire; nine parts copper and one part tin
items.explanation: Bronze Age smiths smelted Welsh copper and Cornish tin before casting bronze tools in two-piece moulds.

items.question: Why did wooden axe handles, plant-fibre cloth, porridge, and Britain's oldest wheel survive at Must Farm (c. 900 BC)?
items.answer: Burning stilt roundhouses fell straight into thick, airless wet river mud so nothing rotted away
items.explanation: Waterlogged Cambridgeshire river silt sealed Must Farm like a time capsule, earning it the nickname "Britain's Pompeii."

items.question: How did Bronze Age builders fasten the thick oak planks of the Dover Boat to cross the English Channel?
items.answer: They stitched the oak planks together using twisted yew branches and sealed seams with moss
items.explanation: Unearthed in Kent in 1992, the sewn-plank Dover Boat carried Bronze Age crews and trade cargoes between Britain and France.

current_items.question: Why could Iron Age blacksmiths make far more tools from iron after 800 BC than earlier smiths could make from bronze?
current_items.answer: Reddish iron ore rock was common across Britain, whereas tin and copper were rare
current_items.explanation: Widespread iron ore meant local village blacksmiths could hammer tough ploughshares, saws, and sickles for everyday farmers.

current_items.question: What was an Iron Age "rotary quern", and how did it work?
current_items.answer: A round stone hand-mill spun with a wooden handle to grind grain into flour
current_items.explanation: Spinning two round millstones ground wheat and barley far faster than rubbing flat saddle stones back and forth.

current_items.question: How did Celtic families build the walls of their cone-roofed thatched roundhouses?
current_items.answer: Wattle and daub (woven hazel sticks plastered thickly with mud, clay, and straw)
current_items.explanation: Wattle-and-daub walls kept heat inside while hearth smoke filtered gently through the thatched roof without a chimney.

current_items.question: Name the giant multi-ringed Iron Age hillfort in Dorset and the famous chalk hill figure in Oxfordshire.
current_items.answer: Maiden Castle in Dorset and the Uffington White Horse in Oxfordshire
current_items.explanation: Maiden Castle's huge chalk ramparts protected hundreds of villagers, while tribes scoured gleaming white chalk into the Uffington Horse.

current_items.question: What were twisted gold "torcs" and stamped gold "staters", and what ended British prehistory in AD 43?
current_items.answer: Heavy twisted gold neck rings and Celtic gold coins; Emperor Claudius's Roman invasion in AD 43
current_items.explanation: Treasures like the Snettisham Great Torc and gold staters flourished right before Roman legions brought written rule in AD 43.

narrative_blocks.title: Blacksmiths, Iron Ploughs & Cosy Roundhouses (c. 800–400 BC)
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.1] Around **800 BC**, clever metalworkers mastered a tough new metal that began Britain's **Iron Age**. Unlike rare tin and copper, reddish **iron ore** rock lay widely across British hills and bogs. **Blacksmiths** heated iron ore in roaring clay furnaces and hammered glowing iron into saws, swords, and **ploughshares**.

[6.2] Strong iron ploughs sliced heavy clay soil easily, helping **Celtic** farmers grow bumper wheat harvests. Families spun round **rotary quern** stones to grind grain into soft flour. They lived inside warm thatched **roundhouses** with **wattle-and-daub** walls of woven sticks and mud. Inside, weavers made bright checked wool on **upright looms**. Hearth smoke drifted gently out through the tall roof.

narrative_blocks.title: Celtic Tribes & Giant Hillforts Like Maiden Castle (c. 400–100 BC)
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.3] As harvests grew, Britain's population boomed and proud **Celtic tribes** competed fiercely for land and cattle. Across high ridges, tribes dug giant **hillforts**, which were hilltop towns ringed by earth banks and ditches! At **Maiden Castle** in Dorset, white chalk **ramparts** rose like giant ocean waves.

[6.4] Maze-like gateways and timber fences forced attackers past defenders armed with smooth river **slingshot** stones. Inside hillforts, hundreds of villagers stored grain in pits, traded sheep, and hammered red-hot iron. In Oxfordshire, tribes even carved the giant **Uffington White Horse** into gleaming white chalk high above the green valley!

narrative_blocks.title: Twisted Gold Torcs, Coins & Rome Arrives (c. 100 BC–AD 43)
narrative_blocks.text:
[6.5] Iron Age Britain shone with dazzling art, brave warriors, and wise priests called **Druids**. Master smiths twisted gold wires into heavy neck rings called **torcs**, like the **Snettisham Great Torc**! Craftworkers also beat ceremonial bronze **horned helmets** and swirling shields. Families offered many treasures into the sacred **River Thames**.

[6.6] By **50 BC**, tribal rulers stamped galloping horses onto gold **stater** coins. Merchants traded British grain, hunting dogs, and tin across the sea with **Gaul** and **Rome**. Then, in **AD 43**, **Emperor Claudius** sent four **Roman legions** across the Channel! Over **800,000 years** of British **prehistory** ended as written history began.

tasks.title: 1. Primary Evidence Detective
tasks.question: Look closely at the round stone with a hole in Source A. How did families use it?
tasks.starter: Looking closely at Source A, Iron Age families poured grain into the central hole of a rotary quern stone so they could...
hints: Identify Source A as the heavy spinning top stone of an Iron Age rotary quern.
Describe pouring wheat or barley into the central hole and turning a wooden peg handle.
Explain why spinning a round quern ground flour much faster than rubbing stones back and forth.
tasks.model_answer: Looking closely at Source A, Iron Age families poured grain into the central hole of a rotary quern stone so they could grind wheat and barley into soft flour. Turning the heavy top stone round and round with a wooden handle crushed grain far faster than older rubbing stones, feeding growing Celtic villages!

tasks.title: 2. Historical Investigation
tasks.question: How did iron ploughshares and rotary querns lead to booming populations and giant hillforts like Maiden Castle?
tasks.starter: Iron tools changed the whole British landscape because widespread iron ore...
hints: Explain how iron ploughshares cut heavy clay soil to grow more wheat, and how Source A (the rotary quern) ground flour faster.
Connect bigger harvests -> more people -> rival Celtic tribes building earth banks and ditches around hillforts like Maiden Castle!
Explain how hillforts worked as busy market and craft towns in peacetime as well as strongholds in war.
tasks.model_answer: Iron tools changed the whole British landscape because widespread iron ore let blacksmiths hammer tough iron ploughshares for every village. Slicing deep clay soils grew bumper harvests of wheat, which families spun quickly into flour using round rotary quern stones. Bigger harvests fed a booming population, so rival Celtic tribes built towering chalk ramparts and maze-like gates at hillforts like Maiden Castle both to defend cattle with slingshots and to gather safely for markets and smithing!

tasks.title: 3. Mission Challenge • The Big Question
tasks.question: Big Question: How did iron tools, hillforts, and Celtic craftwork transform Britain before the Romans arrived in AD 43?
tasks.starter: Across more than 800,000 years from the Stone Age to the Iron Age, the greatest transformation was...
hints: Compare Old/Middle Stone Age hunter-gatherers (Doggerland, Star Carr) with New Stone Age farmers (Skara Brae, Stonehenge).
Compare Bronze Age casting (copper + tin, Must Farm's wheel) with Iron Age blacksmiths, roundhouses, Maiden Castle, and gold coins.
Decide YOUR winner — starting to farm around 4000 BC OR mastering bronze and iron metals — and prove your choice with clear evidence!
tasks.model_answer: Across more than 800,000 years from the Stone Age to the Iron Age, Britain changed from tiny bands of Ice Age hunter-gatherers tracking mammoths across Doggerland into bustling Iron Age tribal kingdoms! Starting to farm around 4000 BC let families settle in stone homes like Skara Brae and raise Stonehenge, while Bronze Age smiths cast recyclable axes, built Must Farm's wheeled carts, and paddled the Dover Boat. Finally, widespread iron ploughs after 800 BC fed thousands inside roundhouses and giant hillforts like Maiden Castle, minting gold coins right as Rome arrived in AD 43!

key_individuals.name: Cheddar Man (c. 8000 BC)
key_individuals.role: Mesolithic Hunter-Gatherer & Britain's Oldest Nearly Complete Human Skeleton
key_individuals.origins: Lived around 10,000 years ago during the Middle Stone Age (Mesolithic), hunting red deer, wild boar, and gathering hazelnuts across the wooded limestone cliffs of Cheddar Gorge in Somerset.
key_individuals.significance: Discovered deep inside cool Gough's Cave in 1903, Cheddar Man preserved ancient DNA inside his inner-ear bone that gave scientists a remarkable window into Britain's earliest post-Ice-Age hunter-gatherers.
achievements: Survived in Britain while Doggerland still joined eastern England to mainland Europe and dense birch and pine forests spread north.
Ancient DNA extracted by Natural History Museum scientists in 2018 indicated dark-to-black skin, dark curly hair, and striking blue-green eyes.
Bone clues showed he died in his early twenties and could not yet digest fresh cow's milk — thousands of years before farming arrived.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Cool, steady limestone cave air inside Gough's Cave protected his fragile skeleton and ancient DNA for 10,000 years!

key_individuals.name: The Star Carr Hunter-Gatherers (c. 9000 BC)
key_individuals.role: Mesolithic Lakeside Camp Builders, Carpenters & Makers of Britain's Oldest Ritual Masks
key_individuals.origins: Extended hunter-gatherer families who camped beside cold, reed-fringed Lake Flixton in the Vale of Pickering, North Yorkshire, shortly after the great Ice Age glaciers melted.
key_individuals.significance: Peat mud at Star Carr preserved Britain's oldest known wooden house post-holes, lakeside timber platforms, barbed antler spear-points, and 21 mysterious carved red-deer skull headdresses.
achievements: Split and shaped birch and aspen tree trunks around 9000 BC — the oldest surviving evidence of carpentry anywhere in Europe!
Carved 21 red-deer skulls with smoothed eye-holes and tie-straps, worn either for sacred dances or for stalking wild deer silently.
Kept tame domestic dogs, paddled wooden canoes, and sparked fires using iron-pyrite strike-a-lights and dried tree fungi.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Proved that Middle Stone Age families were not just wandering cave-dwellers — they built wooden homes and wooden lakeside walkways 6,000 years before Stonehenge!

key_individuals.name: The Skara Brae Villagers (c. 3100–2500 BC)
key_individuals.role: Neolithic Farming Families Who Built Britain's Best-Preserved Stone Age Village
key_individuals.origins: Tight-knit New Stone Age farming and fishing families living beside the Bay of Skaill on the windswept Orkney Islands off northern Scotland — older than both Stonehenge's sarsen circle and Egypt's Great Pyramid!
key_individuals.significance: Because windy Orkney had almost no tall trees, villagers crafted cosy sunken houses, roofed passageways, and complete indoor furniture from flat coastal flagstones — buried safely under sand until a storm in 1850.
achievements: Built eight linked stone houses equipped with stone box beds, central peat hearths, water-tight fish-bait tanks, and shelved stone dressers.
Engineered an indoor stone drainage system linking small side cubicles inside their homes over 5,000 years ago!
Grew hardy barley, herded cattle and sheep, baked Grooved Ware clay pots, and carved mysterious stone balls and bone jewellery.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Walking into House 7 at Skara Brae feels like visiting neighbours who stepped out yesterday — their stone beds and dresser shelves still stand in place!

key_individuals.name: The Amesbury Archer (c. 2300 BC)
key_individuals.role: Alpine-Born Beaker Metalworker & Richest Early Bronze Age Burial in Britain
key_individuals.origins: Born around 2340 BC near the cold, snowy Alps in central Europe; travelled across land and sea as an adult bringing treasured Beaker customs and early metalworking expertise to Salisbury Plain.
key_individuals.significance: Excavated in 2002 just three miles from Stonehenge with over 100 grave goods — five times more items than almost any other burial of his era — proving Early Bronze Age Britain welcomed skilled European newcomers.
achievements: Buried with five comb-stamped Bell Beaker clay pots, three copper knives, sixteen barbed flint arrowheads, and polished stone archer wrist-guards.
Owned a dark cushion-stone anvil used by goldsmiths alongside a pair of coiled sheet-gold hair rings — the oldest dated gold objects in Britain!
Lived into his late thirties or forties despite a painful shattered left kneecap, showing his community cared for and respected him deeply.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Chemical clues from childhood mountain water locked inside his tooth enamel solved a 4,300-year-old mystery by proving he grew up near the Alps!

key_individuals.name: The Must Farm Families (c. 900 BC)
key_individuals.role: Late Bronze Age Stilt-House Builders, Weavers & Makers of Britain's Oldest Wheel
key_individuals.origins: Skilled Fenland families who raised a palisaded ring of timber roundhouses on oak stilts above a slow Cambridgeshire river beside the ancient Flag Fen causeway around 900 BC.
key_individuals.significance: When a fierce fire destroyed their brand-new village, everyone escaped alive while their homes dropped into thick, airless wet mud — preserving Britain's richest snapshot of everyday Bronze Age family life.
achievements: Spun and wove lime-bark and flax plant fibres into superfine cloth with thread counts rivalling modern luxury linen.
Crafted Britain's oldest complete 1-metre wooden cart wheel from ash planks, alongside willow eel traps and hafted socketed bronze axes.
Stacked kitchens with decorated clay bowls, wooden porridge spoons, lamb and venison joints, and exotic glass beads traded from the Mediterranean.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Nicknamed "Britain's Pompeii" because river mud froze one ordinary mealtime — right down to a wooden spoon left inside burnt wheat porridge!

key_individuals.name: Iron Age Celtic Craftworkers & Chieftains (c. 400 BC–AD 43)
key_individuals.role: Tribal Rulers, Hillfort Engineers, Master Smiths & Mint-Makers on the Eve of Rome
key_individuals.origins: Proud regional tribes — such as the Iceni in East Anglia, Durotriges around Maiden Castle in Dorset, and Atrebates and Catuvellauni in the south-east — governed by warrior kings, queens, and Druids.
key_individuals.significance: Transformed Britain with iron ploughs, bustling hilltop strongholds, world-famous swirling Celtic metalwork, and Britain's earliest stamped coinage before Emperor Claudius's Roman invasion in AD 43.
achievements: Engineered colossal earth-and-chalk hillforts like Maiden Castle and scoured iconic chalk landmarks like the 110-metre Uffington White Horse.
Forged tough iron tools and created masterpieces of European art including the Snettisham Great Torc, Battersea Shield, and Waterloo Horned Helmet.
Minted gold and silver stater coins stamped with horses, wheat ears, and royal names while trading peacefully across the Channel with Gaul and Rome.
key_individuals.key_distinction: Shattered Roman propaganda about "backward Britons" forever — proving Iron Age Britain was a land of rich farms, giant forts, and dazzling goldsmiths!
